To enjoy the outdoors, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Purchase a high-quality weather-resistant tent (2 hours)
Step 2. Research local hiking trail maps and elevation gains (3 hours)
Step 3. Relax in a hammock by the lakeshore (4 hours)
Step 4. Pack a cooler with perishable food and ice (45 minutes)
Step 5. Drive to the remote mountain trailhead (3 hours)
Step 6. Check the regional three-day weather forecast (10 minutes)
Step 7. Set up the campsite and pitch the tent (1 hour)
Step 8. Spray hiking boots with waterproof sealant (15 minutes)
Step 9. Charge the portable GPS unit (6 hours)
Step 10. Reserve a specific campsite in the national park (20 minutes)
Step 11. Stop at the ranger station to pick up a wilderness permit (30 minutes)
Step 12. Download offline topographic maps to a smartphone (20 minutes)
Step 13. Fill all hydration bladders and water bottles (15 minutes)
Step 14. Organize the trunk of the car for easy access (30 minutes)
Step 15. Lay out sleeping bags and pillows inside the tent (20 minutes)
Step 16. Secure all food in bear-proof canisters (15 minutes)
Step 17. Load all heavy gear into the vehicle (40 minutes)
Step 18. Purchase a durable camping stove and fuel canisters (1 hour)
Step 19. Check the pressure in the vehicle's spare tire (10 minutes)
Step 20. Double-check that the compass is in the side pocket (5 minutes)
Step 21. Withdraw emergency cash from an ATM (10 minutes)
Step 22. Create a comprehensive weekend trip itinerary (2 hours)
Step 23. Pack a basic first-aid kit with bandages and antiseptic (20 minutes)
Step 24. Perform a final safety sweep of the house before leaving (15 minutes)
Step 25. Calibrate the GPS altitude sensor (5 minutes)
Step 26. Test the tent zippers and rainfly for defects (30 minutes)
Step 27. Buy a bundle of locally sourced firewood (10 minutes)
Step 28. Visit a sporting goods store for specialized gear (1.5 hours)
Step 29. Hang the bear canisters from a high tree branch (30 minutes)
Step 30. Check that the car has a full tank of gasoline (15 minutes)
Step 31. Apply a base layer of sunscreen (10 minutes)
Step 32. Wash and dry all camping clothes (2 hours)
Step 33. Lace up hiking boots for the first trek (5 minutes)
Step 34. Inventory all existing camping supplies in the garage (1 hour)
Step 35. Adjust the side mirrors for a fully loaded car (2 minutes)
Step 36. Inspect the vehicle's fluid levels and oil (20 minutes)
Step 37. Build a controlled campfire in the designated pit (45 minutes)
Step 38. Prepare a simple trail meal over the stove (30 minutes)
Step 39. Confirm the dog-friendly status of the park (10 minutes)
Step 40. Gather dry kindling and small twigs (20 minutes)

You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.
   - BAD (missing some predicates — planner can skip steps with no successors):

     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.
   - BAD (missing some predicates — planner can skip steps with no successors):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (departure_prepared)))
     ; ← missing (luggage_packed), (taxi_called), etc.
     ```
   - GOOD (every action's done predicate required):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

10. Every action's `:duration` MUST come from the time stated in the problem for that step.
    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.
    Do NOT split a step into "the real work" + a 1-second "state confirmation" action —
    `X_done` is simply an effect of the step's action, not a separate action.
    - BAD (the act of "buying beer" is given 1 second; its real duration is absorbed into prior steps):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 1)   :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ; "buy_beer" should have the duration from the problem, not 1 second
      ```
    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 60)  :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ```

11. A `:durative-action` may only have ONE `:condition` keyword. If multiple conditions are needed,
    wrap them ALL in a single `(and ...)` block. Never write multiple separate `:condition` lines.
    - BAD (PDDL parsers only keep the last `:condition`, silently dropping all others):
      ```
      :condition (at start (supplies_obtained))
      :condition (at start (task_pending))
      ```
    - GOOD:
      ```
      :condition (and (at start (supplies_obtained)) (at start (task_pending)))
      ```

12. The number of `:durative-actions` MUST exactly equal the number of steps (one action per step).
    Never generate more or fewer actions than steps — extra actions let the planner skip the most
    expensive one. Correspondingly, initialize exactly N `_pending` predicates in `:init`.
    - BAD (7 actions but only 6 pending predicates initialized — planner ignores the slowest):
      ```
      (:init (a_pending) (b_pending) (c_pending) (d_pending) (e_pending) (f_pending))
      ; assemble_X (1200s) has no a_pending in :init, so the planner never runs it
      ```
    - GOOD (7 actions → 7 pending predicates in :init):
      ```
      (:init (a_pending) (b_pending) (c_pending) (d_pending) (e_pending) (f_pending) (g_pending))
      ```

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```

     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))

       :condition (at start (b_pending))
     ```

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```

       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
     ```

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.

     ```

     ```


    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.

You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.

   - GOOD (every action's done predicate required):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.

    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):

      ```
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 60)  :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ```

You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.
   - BAD (missing some predicates — planner can skip steps with no successors):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (departure_prepared)))
     ; ← missing (luggage_packed), (taxi_called), etc.
     ```
   - GOOD (every action's done predicate required):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

10. Every action's `:duration` MUST come from the time stated in the problem for that step.
    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.
    Do NOT split a step into "the real work" + a 1-second "state confirmation" action —
    `X_done` is simply an effect of the step's action, not a separate action.
    - BAD (the act of "buying beer" is given 1 second; its real duration is absorbed into prior steps):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 1)   :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ; "buy_beer" should have the duration from the problem, not 1 second
      ```
    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 60)  :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ```

11. A `:durative-action` may only have ONE `:condition` keyword. If multiple conditions are needed,
    wrap them ALL in a single `(and ...)` block. Never write multiple separate `:condition` lines.
    - BAD (PDDL parsers only keep the last `:condition`, silently dropping all others):
      ```
      :condition (at start (supplies_obtained))
      :condition (at start (task_pending))
      ```
    - GOOD:
      ```
      :condition (and (at start (supplies_obtained)) (at start (task_pending)))
      ```

12. The number of `:durative-actions` MUST exactly equal the number of steps (one action per step).

    expensive one. Correspondingly, initialize exactly N `_pending` predicates in `:init`.

    - GOOD (7 actions → 7 pending predicates in :init):
      ```
      (:init (a_pending) (b_pending) (c_pending) (d_pending) (e_pending) (f_pending) (g_pending))
      ```

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     ```

   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

8. Every action MUST:

You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.

   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`

   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.

5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.

7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

     ```
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

     ```

       :condition (at start (b_pending))
     ```

    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.

You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.
   - BAD (missing some predicates — planner can skip steps with no successors):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (departure_prepared)))
     ; ← missing (luggage_packed), (taxi_called), etc.
     ```
   - GOOD (every action's done predicate required):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

10. Every action's `:duration` MUST come from the time stated in the problem for that step.
    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.
    Do NOT split a step into "the real work" + a 1-second "state confirmation" action —
    `X_done` is simply an effect of the step's action, not a separate action.
    - BAD (the act of "buying beer" is given 1 second; its real duration is absorbed into prior steps):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 1)   :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ; "buy_beer" should have the duration from the problem, not 1 second
      ```
    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 60)  :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ```

11. A `:durative-action` may only have ONE `:condition` keyword. If multiple conditions are needed,
    wrap them ALL in a single `(and ...)` block. Never write multiple separate `:condition` lines.
    - BAD (PDDL parsers only keep the last `:condition`, silently dropping all others):
      ```
      :condition (at start (supplies_obtained))
      :condition (at start (task_pending))
      ```
    - GOOD:
      ```
      :condition (and (at start (supplies_obtained)) (at start (task_pending)))
      ```

12. The number of `:durative-actions` MUST exactly equal the number of steps (one action per step).

    expensive one. Correspondingly, initialize exactly N `_pending` predicates in `:init`.

    - GOOD (7 actions → 7 pending predicates in :init):
      ```

      ```

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.

Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```

       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
     ```

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.


You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.
   - BAD (missing some predicates — planner can skip steps with no successors):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (departure_prepared)))
     ; ← missing (luggage_packed), (taxi_called), etc.
     ```
   - GOOD (every action's done predicate required):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

10. Every action's `:duration` MUST come from the time stated in the problem for that step.
    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.
    Do NOT split a step into "the real work" + a 1-second "state confirmation" action —
    `X_done` is simply an effect of the step's action, not a separate action.
    - BAD (the act of "buying beer" is given 1 second; its real duration is absorbed into prior steps):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 1)   :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ; "buy_beer" should have the duration from the problem, not 1 second
      ```
    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 60)  :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ```

    wrap them ALL in a single `(and ...)` block. Never write multiple separate `:condition` lines.
    - BAD (PDDL parsers only keep the last `:condition`, silently dropping all others):

    - GOOD:

      ```
      :condition (and (at start (supplies_obtained)) (at start (task_pending)))
      ```

    - GOOD (7 actions → 7 pending predicates in :init):


You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.
   - BAD (missing some predicates — planner can skip steps with no successors):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (departure_prepared)))

     ```
   - GOOD (every action's done predicate required):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.
    Do NOT split a step into "the real work" + a 1-second "state confirmation" action —

    - BAD (the act of "buying beer" is given 1 second; its real duration is absorbed into prior steps):

    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):
      ```

      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 60)  :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ```

You are a PDDL expert. Given an asynchronous planning problem, write the domain and problem files in minimal PDDL 2.1 format.

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors need only `(at start (X_pending))` in their condition.

9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include ALL `_done` predicates (one per action).
   This ensures the planner cannot skip any step.
   - BAD (missing some predicates — planner can skip steps with no successors):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (departure_prepared)))
     ; ← missing (luggage_packed), (taxi_called), etc.
     ```
   - GOOD (every action's done predicate required):
     ```
     (:goal (and (tickets_booked) (luggage_packed) (taxi_called) ... (departure_prepared)))
     ```

10. Every action's `:duration` MUST come from the time stated in the problem for that step.
    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.
    Do NOT split a step into "the real work" + a 1-second "state confirmation" action —
    `X_done` is simply an effect of the step's action, not a separate action.
    - BAD (the act of "buying beer" is given 1 second; its real duration is absorbed into prior steps):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 1)   :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ; "buy_beer" should have the duration from the problem, not 1 second
      ```
    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money  :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer    :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 60)  :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ```

11. A `:durative-action` may only have ONE `:condition` keyword. If multiple conditions are needed,
    wrap them ALL in a single `(and ...)` block. Never write multiple separate `:condition` lines.
    - BAD (PDDL parsers only keep the last `:condition`, silently dropping all others):
      ```
      :condition (at start (supplies_obtained))
      :condition (at start (task_pending))
      ```
    - GOOD:
      ```
      :condition (and (at start (supplies_obtained)) (at start (task_pending)))
      ```

12. The number of `:durative-actions` MUST exactly equal the number of steps (one action per step).
    Never generate more or fewer actions than steps — extra actions let the planner skip the most
    expensive one. Correspondingly, initialize exactly N `_pending` predicates in `:init`.
    - BAD (7 actions but only 6 pending predicates initialized — planner ignores the slowest):

      ```
      ; assemble_X (1200s) has no a_pending in :init, so the planner never runs it
      ```
    - GOOD (7 actions → 7 pending predicates in :init):
      ```
      (:init (a_pending) (b_pending) (c_pending) (d_pending) (e_pending) (f_pending) (g_pending))
      ```

Step 21. Group the orchid with other tropical plants (10 minutes)
Step 22. Trim away any dead or dried flower spikes (5 minutes)
Step 23. Purchase a new pot with plenty of drainage holes (45 minutes)

Step 25. Position the orchid in its new light-optimal spot (2 minutes)

Step 27. Clean the leaves with a damp, soft cloth (15 minutes)

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).
Each action gets its own pair of predicates: `(X_pending)` and `(X_done)`.
`X_done` is BOTH the "step completed" marker AND the semantic predicate for successors.

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:typing`, `:negative-preconditions`,
   `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, use a positive "_pending" predicate:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:

8. Every action MUST:
   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be

   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):

     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)

       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

ENCODING: Use PARAMETERLESS actions (no step type, no step objects).

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:

   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`

3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. No `:types` block or `:objects` block is needed — actions take NO parameters.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "_pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

   (a) consume its own `(X_pending)` at start: `(at start (not (X_pending)))`
   (b) produce its own `(X_done)` at end: `(at end (X_done))`
   (c) require ALL direct predecessors' `_done` predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```

       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (c_pending)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (c_pending))) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (a_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (a_pending))) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (b_pending))
       :effect (and (at start (not (b_pending))) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :parameters () :duration (= ?duration 600)
     ```

To learn to body surf, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Purchase a pair of high-quality swim fins (45 minutes)
Step 2. Research the best local beaches for beginners (1 hour)
Step 3. Practice the "handplane" lead arm position in the water (30 minutes)
Step 4. Watch instructional videos on wave mechanics (2 hours)
Step 5. Practice holding your breath underwater for extended periods (1 week)
Step 6. Apply waterproof sunscreen to your back and shoulders (10 minutes)
Step 7. Buy a comfortable, snug-fitting swim suit (1 hour)
Step 8. Pack a gear bag with towels and water (15 minutes)
Step 9. Learn how to identify a "spilling" wave vs a "plunging" wave (3 hours)
Step 10. Practice the "streamline" body position on dry land (20 minutes)
Step 11. Perform core strengthening exercises to improve stability (2 weeks)
Step 12. Check the local tide charts and swell forecast (15 minutes)
Step 13. Read about ocean safety and rip currents (2 hours)
Step 14. Do a dynamic warm-up on the sand (15 minutes)
Step 15. Enroll in a basic ocean swimming fitness course (1 month)
Step 16. Practice kicking efficiently with fins in a pool (3 days)
Step 17. Find a mentor or experienced body surfer to shadow (2 days)
Step 18. Attempt to catch your first small whitewater wave (1 hour)
Step 19. Watch the locals to see where they are catching waves (30 minutes)
Step 20. Practice duck-diving under oncoming waves (2 hours)
Step 21. Execute a full ride from the peak to the shore (5 minutes)
Step 22. Observe the rhythm of the sets from the shoreline (45 minutes)
Step 23. Look up the history of traditional Hawaiian body surfing (1 hour)
Step 24. Wade out to the chest-deep break zone (10 minutes)
Step 25. Drive to the beach (45 minutes)
Step 26. Wake up early to beat the crowds (5 minutes)
Step 27. Read a book on advanced wave riding techniques (4 days)
Step 28. Learn how to exit a wave safely before it closes out (1 hour)
Step 29. Map out the driving route to the coast (10 minutes)
Step 30. Check the weather report for offshore winds (5 minutes)
Step 31. Put on your swim gear (10 minutes)
Step 32. Practice treading water in deep sections (2 days)
Step 33. Practice the "kick-off" launch from a standing position (1 hour)
Step 34. Secure your car keys in a waterproof pouch (5 minutes)
Step 35. Buy a pair of fin tethers to prevent losing them (30 minutes)
Step 36. Attach the fin tethers to your ankles (5 minutes)
Step 37. Apply anti-chafe balm under your arms (5 minutes)
Step 38. Rinse your fins in fresh water (5 minutes)
Step 39. Walk from the parking lot to the sand (10 minutes)
